activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Connor wanted to build a tall tower. His tower fell down. It fell fast. Connor sat on the floor and began to wonder. Why did it fall?

"Try a big block at the bottom," said Mom.

Connor put a big block at the bottom. He put small blocks on top. The tower stood up. It did not fall. Big blocks made the tower strong. Small blocks made it tall.

Mom brought hot cocoa. "Careful, it is hot," she said. She held the cup for him. Connor blew on it. The cocoa got cool. He took one slow sip. "It was hot. Now it is cold," he said.

Then his hands were dirty from the blocks. Mom gave him a small towel, a good tool for messy hands. He wiped them clean.

"Can I make another tower?" Connor asked.

"Yes," said Mom. "Make it big." Connor stacked the blocks high.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Asher ran to the park with Mama. He wanted to find the big red slide. "Stay close to me," said Mama. Asher held her hand.

They walked past a grill. The grill made sizzling sounds. Asher saw steam rise up. "That is hot," said Mama. She put her hand out. Asher stopped. The grill was for the man with the hot dogs. Only the man touched it. Asher watched from far away. Then he saw it. The man touched the grill, and the hot dogs got warm. Hot things made other things hot.

Asher found a shiny bottle on the grass. He reached down. "Not that," said Mama softly. "We do not touch bottles we find." She picked it up and put it in the bin. Asher clapped. He loved helping.

Then came the surprise. The man from the grill walked over. He gave Asher a warm hot dog in a bun. Asher took it to the picnic table. Mama brought his cup of juice. Asher sat close to her and took a big bite. "Happy!" said Asher, with juice in his hand and Mama by his side.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Isiah sat in his car seat. His tummy felt funny. "I want my milk," he said.

"It is at home," said Mama. "It is cold there."

A big truck went by. Vroom! It was fast. Their car was slow. Isaiah clapped. "The truck wins, Mama!"

Then they stopped. A little red car pulled up. It was small. Their car was big. Isaiah laughed. "We are big!"

Sun came in the window. It made Isaiah's arm warm. "Hot," he said. He moved his arm away. Then he touched the cold window glass with one finger. "Brrr!"

They got home. Mama took the milk from the big fridge. She gave Isaiah the cup. He drank it all down.

"Cold milk," said Isaiah. He gave Mama a big hug. "More tomorrow?"

"Yes," said Mama. "More tomorrow."

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Raphael sat in the big chair at the dentist. He was waiting for his turn. His tummy felt hungry. Mama had brought apple slices for after.

"First we wash hands," said the friendly nurse. She took Raphael to the little sink. She gave him soap. Raphael rubbed the soap on his hands. Bubbles grew and grew. He rubbed and rubbed. The nurse sang a song while he rubbed. The song had two parts.

Raphael looked at his hands. The sticky jam from breakfast was gone. The bubbles had carried it away down the sink. He held his hands up to the light. They were clean and shiny.

Then Raphael got his apple slices. He ate them in the middle of the waiting room. No jam, no dirt, just apple. He licked his fingers. They still smelled like soap.

After his checkup, Raphael went to the toilet. Then he ran back to the sink. "Soap please!" he said. He rubbed the bubbles all over again. A small boy watched him from the door.

"Look," said Raphael. He showed his clean hands. "Now you try." The boy got soap too. They sang the song together. Then the boy skipped back to his mama, holding his clean hands up high.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Eva stands with her dad. The big yellow bus comes around the corner. It stops with a soft hiss. The doors fold open.

Eva climbs up. One step, two steps, three steps. She finds a seat by the window. The glass is cold on her nose.

A car stops next to the bus. A little dog sits inside it. The dog has a pink nose. Eva taps the window. The dog wags its tail. She taps again. The dog barks. She laughs and taps one more time. The dog's ears go up.

The glass is foggy now. Eva writes on it with her finger. She makes a wobbly letter E. Then the bus starts to move, and the dog slides out of sight, tail still wagging.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Arlo sat at the big table. He wanted to make a garden picture. He had paper, glue, and little paper flowers.

Arlo put glue on a flower. He pushed it onto the paper. It stuck! "It stays," he said.

He put glue on another flower. Then more glue. Then more. Now the paper was very slippery. The flower slid down, down, down. It landed at the bottom. "Oh no," said Arlo. "My flower slid away!"

Would a little glue work better? He could guess and try. Arlo put on a small dot of glue. He pressed one flower. It stayed. He pressed another flower. It stayed too.

"One flower, two flowers, three flowers," said Arlo. His garden picture grew and grew. All the flowers stayed in place.

Mama came to look. Arlo held it up high. "Look at my garden!"

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Avery sat at the little red table. She wanted to paint a picture of her pet cat. The cat was yellow with white paws.

She found the yellow paint first. She made a round yellow body on the paper. "Good," said her teacher, Miss Kim. "Now you need green eyes."

Avery looked for green. She could not find it. Then she saw Ben using the green pot. She waited, but Ben tipped the pot over. Green paint spilled across the table.

"Be careful," said Miss Kim. She wiped up the green spill with a cloth. Then she scooped some green paint into a small cup for Avery.

Avery painted two green eyes. Then she painted a red ball next to the cat. The cat in the picture looked just like her pet at home.

"Meow," said Avery, and she held the paper up high.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
story:
Elizabeth stood by the classroom door. Her coat was zipped up to her chin. Her tummy felt jumpy. She wanted to see her mama, but mama was gone.

A boy sat on the rug. He was crying. His shoe was stuck in a puddle of glue. Elizabeth looked at the glue. Then she looked at her shoe. She stepped on the sticky spot too. Her shoe stuck, just like his.

She pulled hard. Her shoe came off. She sat down and looked at it. The glue was slimy on the bottom. She rubbed her shoe on the rug. The glue came off, little by little. She picked up the boy's shoe too. She rubbed it on the rug the same way.

The boy stopped crying. He put his shoe back on. "Thank you," he said. Elizabeth smiled. Then she unzipped her coat all by herself. She hung it on a little hook with her name on it. The teacher gave them each a red crayon. Elizabeth drew a big sun. The boy drew a sun right next to hers.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Beau sat in his car seat. He wanted his blue toy truck. It was not in the bag.

"Let's look for it," said Mom. The car went down the road. Beau looked out the window.

"I see a cow!" said Beau. The cow stood by a fence. Then he saw a sheep. Then a dog. "Animals, animals!" said Beau.

"Look in your lunch bag," said Mom. Beau found his banana. He found his crackers. He found his juice. "Food!" said Beau. Still no truck.

The wind blew on the window. It was windy outside. A leaf flew up, up, up. Beau laughed.

Then the car bumped. Something slid out from under the seat. It was the blue truck!

"Truck!" Beau shouted. He hugged it tight. "You were hiding under the seat."

Mom laughed too. "Truck, you found us," she said.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. On Monday, Myles took him to the park. "Look, Grandpa! Ducks!" said Myles. Grandpa sat down on a bench. He put his hat over his face. Soon his eyes were closed. He was asleep.

Myles wanted the ducks to come close. He clapped his hands. The ducks flew away. Myles clapped again. The ducks went even farther. "Oh no," said Myles.

Then Myles had an idea. He sat still like a rock. He sat still like a rock on the grass. One duck looked at him. It came back. Then two ducks came back. Then five ducks waddled right up to his shoes!

Grandpa woke up. "Look at all those ducks!" he said. "Shh," whispered Myles. "I am a rock." Grandpa sat still like a rock too. The biggest duck looked at them both. Then it nibbled the grass next to Grandpa's big toe.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Nora was at her friend Mia's house. Mia had a tablet. It was dark and still. "Watch this," said Mia. Mia pushed the little round button. The screen lit up! It showed colors and little pictures.

"Can I try?" asked Nora. Mia's mom said yes. Nora pushed the button too. Tap. The light came on again. She tapped the green square with a crayon on it. A white page opened, big and empty. Nora drew a purple cat. Then she drew a messy orange sun. She tapped blue, and the line turned blue. One tap, one new color. How did it know?

Then it was time for a snack. Mia's mom said to put the tablet away. Nora tapped the button and held it. The screen went dark again. She slid it into its cover, like a book going to bed on the shelf.

But wait. The cover had a little flap. Nora lifted it, and there was the tablet's name written inside. "It has a name!" said Nora. "Mine is called Pickle," said Mia. Nora smiled and patted the cover gently. "Night night, Pickle," she said.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Paisley ran down the sidewalk. The bookmobile was here! The big blue truck had shelves and shelves of books inside.

"Today you get your very own library card," said Mama. "Your very first one."

Paisley jumped up and down. She picked out a book about a red fire truck. The cover felt rough on her fingers. The librarian typed Paisley's name into her computer. Then she handed Paisley a little white card. Paisley held it with both hands. It was hers, all hers!

"Now the book is yours to take home," said the librarian. "But you must bring it back. Another girl wants the fire truck book too."

"No," said Paisley. "I want to keep it forever and ever."

"Let's walk home and read it first," said Mama.

Paisley read the fire truck book at breakfast. She read it in her tent. She read it to her teddy bear. Then on Saturday, they saw the girl from the bookmobile at the park. The girl was holding a book about fire trucks. It was not the same one. It was a different one, and she looked sad.

"The bookmobile book," the girl said. "You have the fire truck one. I am next."

Paisley ran all the way home. "Mama! Mama! We have to walk back to the bookmobile!"

They found the big blue truck. Paisley gave the book to the librarian. The librarian gave it to the girl. The girl hugged the fire truck book tight.

"Thank you," she said. "Now I get my turn!"

"And next week," said the librarian, "you can pick a new book, Paisley. A green dinosaur book came in today."

Paisley grinned. "Next week," she said. "Next week, next week!"

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Lennon went to the cultural center with Mama and Papa. There was a big table of paper lanterns. Each lantern had a little candle inside. Lennon wanted to send her lantern down the little water path, like the other kids.

Papa lit her candle with a long match. Then the wind came in the door. Whoosh. The little flame went out. The room felt dark on her side. Lennon frowned. Her lantern looked wrong with no light.

Mama held her hands around the flame. Papa lit it again. The flame stood up straight. "Your hands stop the wind," said Mama. So Lennon put her hands around it too. She cupped them like a tiny house. The flame did not go out this time.

Lennon walked to the water. She set her lantern down. It floated away, warm and bright. She watched it go. "Bye bye, lantern," she said. She waved and waved.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Lucy went to the park with Gran. The sun was out. It was sunny. Lucy wore her sun hat. "My hat keeps my head cool," she said.

Then the wind came. The wind blew Lucy's hat off! It rolled on the grass. Gran ran and got it. "It is windy now," said Gran. "Put on your coat." Lucy put on her coat. The wind could not get in.

Then dark clouds came. Rain fell. It was rainy. Gran opened a big umbrella. Lucy stood under it with Gran. "I keep dry here," said Lucy.

Then the rain turned white and soft. It was snowy! Lucy held out her hand. The snow felt cold. Gran put warm mittens on Lucy's hands. "What kind of snow is this?" Lucy asked. "Soft snow," said Gran.

Lucy looked at her hat, her coat, her mittens. All her clothes helped her stay and play. "Same park," said Lucy. "New sky!" Gran laughed and held her hand.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Hailey sat in the cafe with her dad. A kind waiter brought paper and a pencil. "Can you write your name?" Dad asked. Hailey wanted to sign her own picture. She squeezed the pencil in her whole fist. She made marks. The marks looked ugly and wobbly. "H" looked like a squiggle worm.

Dad drew a little crab on a napkin. The crab held a stick with its small claw. Hailey looked at her own hand. She pinched the pencil with two fingers, like a crab claw. She pressed down and made an H. Then an A. The letters stood up straight! She wrote H-A-I-L-E-Y all by herself.

She held up the paper. "I painted my name!" The waiter clapped. Dad gave her hand a soft kiss. "Write it again," he said. Hailey pinched the pencil and wrote it again.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Lily wants to draw a cat on the big tablet. The screen is dark and still. She waits. It stays dark.

Lily taps the screen one time. Nothing happens. She taps it two times. Nothing happens. Then her teacher, Miss Kim, comes over. "Try the little stick," says Miss Kim. She points to the side.

Lily finds the small stick button. She pushes it and holds it. She counts slowly, "One, two, three." The screen lights up. Lily claps her hands.

The tablet has little pictures on it. Lily looks for the drawing one. She taps the crayon picture. The drawing app opens. Now the screen is white and empty. Lily moves her finger on it. A red line goes straight across the screen. She moves her finger again. A round circle appears. That will be the cat's tummy. She adds two ears and a tail.

Then the bell rings. Time to go. Lily taps the crayon picture the way Miss Kim showed her. The app closes. She pushes the little stick and counts, "One, two, three." The screen goes dark. She sets the tablet on the shelf, all neat and straight. "Bye, cat," says Lily. "I will draw you again tomorrow."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Sarah went to the store with Mama. She wanted red apples for a snack. "How many apples do we need?" Mama asked. "Let's guess," said Sarah. "Maybe four!" Mama held the bag. Sarah picked one apple. Then two apples. Then three apples. Then four apples. "Can I count them?" asked Sarah. "Yes," said Mama. "One, two, three, four." Sarah put one apple back. "Now I have three," she said.

At the bread shelf, Sarah saw a song card. It had ten little ducks on it. A boy was singing near it. "One, two, three, four, five," he sang. Sarah listened. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" she sang too. The boy smiled at her.

Sarah saw Mama put coins in a machine. The machine rolled the coins. It made a round shape, like a triangle but round. Then it gave back paper money. "Can I hear it again?" asked Sarah. "Yes," said Mama. She put in more coins. Click, click, click. Sarah laughed. "That is a cute little sound," she said. They walked to the car. Sarah held the apple bag all the way home.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Ibrahim sat in his big seat in the car. They were going to Grandpa's house early in the morning. Ibrahim saw a river out of the window. "The river is so wide," he said. He wanted his water bottle. It had slid far away on the seat.

"Can you help me, please?" Ibrahim asked. Mama reached back and picked up the bottle. "Here you go," she said. "Thank you," said Ibrahim. He took a little drink.

Then the car went over a bump. The bottle jumped and spilled on Mama's coat. "Oh no," said Ibrahim. "Sorry, Mama." Mama smiled at him in the mirror. "That is okay," she said. "It was only a bump."

Ibrahim held the bottle tight with both hands. The car went over another bump. This time nothing spilled. He had held it, so it stayed dry. "Mama, look!" said Ibrahim. He showed her the dry bottle. Mama laughed softly. "You held it so well," she said. Grandpa's door was coming up ahead, and Ibrahim waved through the window.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Lydia stood at the baseball diamond. She held a purple beanbag in her hands. A hoop sat on the grass in front of her. She wanted the beanbag to go in the hoop.

"Throw it low," said Dad.

Lydia threw it high. The beanbag flew over the hoop. It landed in the grass. Dad went to bring it back to her.

"Try again," said Dad. "Nice and easy."

Lydia looked at the hoop. She looked at her hand. She threw the beanbag low and slow. It went in the hoop. It stayed there.

"It went in!" said Lydia. She clapped her hands.

Then Dad brought a big ball. He rolled it to her on the ground. Lydia reached out with one hand. The ball bounced off her fingers. It rolled away.

"Use both hands," said Dad.

Dad rolled the ball again. Lydia held out both hands. The ball bumped right into them. Her two hands closed around it. She held it tight.

"I caught it!" said Lydia.

"Yes, you did," said Dad. "One more time."

Lydia threw the beanbag into the hoop. Then she caught the big ball with both hands. She did it again and again, and the sun went down slowly over the baseball diamond.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Charlie could not find her bear. "Where can he be?" she asked.

Mama smiled. "Look in the bathtub."

Charlie ran to the tub. No bear there. But there was a wet sock. "The bath made you wet!" she told the sock. She hung the sock on the rail. It dripped, dripped, dripped.

Next she looked under her bed. No bear. But there was her plate from snack time. "Oh no," said Charlie. "You still have cheese on you." She carried the plate to the kitchen. Papa washed it. "You are a smart helper," he said.

Then Charlie pulled her pajama shirt over her head. Something soft was inside it. It was bear! "You were in my shirt!" Charlie laughed. "Did you want to sleep in it?" Bear said nothing. Bears are quiet like that.

Mama tucked them both in tight. "Night night, sleepy bear," said Charlie. She closed her eyes and gave him one more hug.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Addison went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about a mean dragon. Dad said, "Let's look for shapes first. Then we find the dragon."

Addison found a rug with a red circle. She put her foot on the circle. The circle was as big as her foot and her hand together. She jumped to a blue square next to it. The square had four sides, like a window.

Then she heard a scratch, scratch, scratch. A toy box was rubbing on the floor. The box was a rectangle, long like a loaf of bread. Addison pushed the box away from the wall. The scratch stopped. She pushed it back. The scratch came back. She laughed. "The box makes that sound!"

A librarian walked by with books stacked high. "That stack looks like a triangle," said Dad. The bottom row was wide. The top had just one book. Addison held up her hands like a triangle too. Her fingers touched at the top.

At last they found the dragon book. The dragon on the cover had a round tummy. "Look," said Addison. "The mean dragon is full of circles!" Dad laughed. They sat down to read. Addison turned the first page.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
James wanted to paint a picture at school. He wanted to paint a green frog. But the paint pots had no green paint.

James looked at the pots. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. James tried the yellow pot first. He made a yellow frog on his paper. The frog did not look right.

Then James had an idea. He let some blue paint drip onto his brush. He mixed the blue with the yellow. He stirred it slowly. The paint turned green! James painted his frog green. He painted a red flower too.

Teacher Mia wrote his name on the paper. Then she hung it up to dry. "My green frog has a name," James said. "His name is Hop."

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Athena wanted pancakes, big ones. Mama poured a big circle of batter. It spread out wide, wide, wide. Then Mama poured a small circle. "That one is for you," Mama said. Athena clapped. The small pancake was just her size.

The big pancake sat on the hot pan. Athena stood far away and watched. It went sizzle, sizzle, sizzle. Bubbles grew on top. When Mama flipped it, it flew up fast, like a flying carpet. Athena gasped. "It's a magic pancake!" she said. "It flies!" Mama smiled and flipped the small one too. It flew up slowly, gently, like a little bird learning to fly.

Mama put the pancakes on plates. They were too hot to touch. "We will wait," said Mama. Athena waited. She wiggled her curly hair with her fingers. Then she touched her cold glass of milk with both hands. The milk was cold like snow. The pancakes slowly stopped steaming.

At last Athena took a tiny bite. It was just right. She ate the small pancake all up. "I helped wait," she said proudly. Her family laughed and ate together. Athena looked at her empty plate and held it up high. "More magic pancakes, please!"

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Beatrice ran to the play corner at school. She wanted to play house with her baby doll, Rose. But Rose was gone! The basket was empty.

Beatrice looked under the table. No Rose. She looked in the toy oven. No Rose. Then she heard a sound. "Ba ba ba." It came from the dress-up box.

Beatrice opened the lid. There was Rose! Tommy had tucked Rose inside a hat. "She is sleeping in her bed," Tommy said. "One hat, one blanket, one baby."

"Rose is hungry," said Beatrice. She held Rose on her lap. She bent a small spoon towards Rose's mouth. She made a pretend pot of soup. "One spoon, two spoops, three spoons," she counted. Rose drank it all up.

Then Rose got a bump. Beatrice kissed the bump. She wrapped Rose in a scarf. "One scarf, one hug, all better," she said.

Tommy put a tiny cup beside Rose. "Tea for baby," he said.

Beatrice smiled a happy smile. The play corner had become a whole house. She rocked Rose to sleep.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Yesterday Milo put a bean seed in a cup of dirt. His teacher, Miss Ada, helped him pat the dirt down. She had a loose tooth that wiggled when she smiled.

Today Milo ran to the window shelf. He looked at his cup. There was only dirt. No bean. No green. He wanted to see his plant now. "Not now," said Miss Ada. "Plants come later. Water it and wait." Milo gave the cup a little drink of water. The dirt turned dark. It went from dry to wet. A woman from the lunch room came by with a tray of cups. "Pay attention to that bean," she said. "My class grew beans when I was small. I watered mine every day." She set a straw by Milo's cup so he could drip the water slow.

Tomorrow morning, Milo came back to school. He looked at his cup. A small green tip was poking up. It was bent like a tiny hook. He had watered the dirt, and now the bean was coming. "Look," he said to Miss Ada. "It came up." She wiggled her loose tooth and clapped her hands. "Let's give it more water," she said.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Lillian had a cold. She caught it from her brother last week. Now she was home, and her nose was all stuffed up.

Lillian wanted to smell her toast. She sniffed and sniffed. She could not smell a thing. That made her sad.

Mama made warm soup on the stove. Steam rose up from the pot. Lillian watched from her chair. Mama set the bowl in front of her. The steam curled under her nose. Lillian breathed it in. Slowly, her nose began to open. Then she smelled the soup. It smelled so good. "I can smell it!" she said.

Lillian slurped the warm soup. Her nose ran a little, so Mama gave her a fresh tissue. Lillian blew, soft and gentle. Then she looked out the window. A plane flew high in the sky. It made a little white line behind it. Lillian sniffed the air again. "Mama, I can smell the toast too," she said. Mama smiled and pushed the plate closer.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
James put his arms in his coat. One arm went in easy. The other arm went in easy too. Now for the zipper.

James pulled the zipper up. Nothing happened. He pulled again. Still nothing. The zipper stayed open and his tummy felt the cold air.

Mom was busy at the bank desk. James wanted to zip it all by himself. He looked down at his coat. What was wrong?

Then James saw it. The little zipper parts were not together at the bottom. One side was up high. One side was down low. Could he fix that?

James sat on the bank bench. He put the pointy zipper tab into the slot at the very bottom. He heard a small click. He touched the tab to make sure.

James pulled the tab up. Zip! The coat closed all the way to his chin. No more cold air on his tummy.

Mom came back. She saw his coat. "Did you do that yourself?" she asked.

James smiled big. "Zip!" he said, and pulled it down, then up again.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Mohamed went to the farmers' market with his mama. He held a loose coin in his little hand. A bird tried to fly away with his bread roll. "Silly bird," laughed Mohamed. "That is my bread!"

Mohamed wanted to bake an apple cake for his family. He picked three red apples from a big crate. "These smell sweet," he said. He sniffed one apple, twice.

At home, Mama peeled the apples with a sharp knife. Mohamed stayed far from the knife. He helped mash the apples in a bowl. He pushed the spoon down. The big apple chunks turned soft and squishy. "Look, Mama," he said. "I push, and they go smush!"

Then Mohamed pressed the dough with his palms. The dough got flat and wide. He patted it like a drum. Papa laughed and said, "Are you fixing a cake or using a hammer?" Mohamed giggled and patted some more.

Mama put the cake in the hot oven. Mohamed watched from his chair. Soon the kitchen smelled like sweet apples. Papa sniffed the air. "Mmm," he said. "Is it ready yet?"

At last the cake came out, golden and warm. Mohamed took a big bite. "I made this," he said. "With apples and smushing and patting." Papa gave him a thumbs up and said, "Best cake ever, little baker."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Rosalie and her family went to the beach. It was far from home. They packed a big bag. Rosalie packed her tiny yellow duck. "Where will we sleep?" she asked. Mom smiled. "We will call Grandma when we get there."

At the beach, the sand was warm. The water went swish, swish up the rocks. Rosalie made a sandcastle. She patted the sand. Pat, pat, pat. Then a wave came. Swish! The wave took her castle away. Rosalie gasped. Where did it go?

She made a new castle. A wave came again. Swish! It was gone again. "The water takes the sand," said Rosalie. She watched the wave pull back. Could she see it pull the sand? She looked close. Yes! Tiny bits of sand moved with the water.

Dad called, "Time to call Grandma!" Rosalie ran to him. She held the phone. "Grandma, the water takes my castle!" she said. Grandma laughed. Rosalie waved at the sea. "Bye bye, water," she said.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Kai sat on Grandma's big red rug. Grandma played her old piano. The song had a steady beat. One, two, one, two.

Kai wanted to clap along. He clapped fast, fast, fast. "Too fast," said Grandma. She stopped the song.

Grandma clapped slow claps. One, two, one, two. She clapped and waited. Kai watched her hands. Then he clapped, too. One, two, one, two. His claps matched the piano. When the song went steady, his claps went steady. When the song stopped, his claps stopped.

"Now sing with me," said Grandma. She sang "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." Kai hummed. He tried again. He hummed the tune. Then came the words. He sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." He did not stop there. "How I wonder what you are." He sang it all by himself.

"Kai, that was like a little gift," said Grandma. "And your claps were not naughty one bit. They were just right." Kai laughed. He patted the piano keys. "Again," he said. Grandma's fingers wiggled like fish that swim in water. "Again," she said. One, two, one, two.

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Jaxon woke up at Grandpa's house. The sun was warm on his blanket. He wanted his teddy bear, Brown Bear. But Brown Bear had a big oatmeal spot on his tummy from breakfast. "Oh dear," said Grandma. "Let's wash him."

Grandma filled the sink with warm, soapy water. Jaxon dipped Brown Bear in. He rubbed the spot with his small hands. The bubbles smelled like flowers. The spot grew lighter and lighter. Then it was gone. "Clean!" said Jaxon.

Grandma carried the wet bear outside. She hung him on the clothes line with two wooden pins. Brown Bear swung in the soft breeze. Jaxon waited on the steps. He knocked on the door to call Grandpa. "Come see!" he said. Grandpa came out, and they waited together.

The sun shone and the wind blew. Soon the fur looked fluffy. Jaxon touched it. Dry! He hugged Brown Bear close. The bear felt warm from the sun. A shy little ladybug sat on the clothes pin. It opened its wings, then flew away. "Bye bye," whispered Jaxon, waving his hand.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Jake went to the library with his mom. He wanted the big dinosaur book. It had shiny teeth on the cover.

A girl named Mia grabbed the book first. Jake grabbed the other side. The book went "boing" between them. The librarian put her finger to her lips. Everyone froze like statues. Jake let go of the book. Then Mia held it out to him. "You first," she said. Jake sat down and turned the pages. The dinosaur looked like it winked at him.

When Jake finished, he slid the book across the rug to Mia. "Your turn," he said. Mia smiled. Then a little bee flew past the window, buzzing like a tiny truck. Jake and Mia watched it together, side by side, sharing the last page of the dinosaur book.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Mason lost his monkey. The monkey had soft arms and a spotted tummy. "Where can he be?" said Mason. He looked under the bed. No monkey. He looked in the toy box. No monkey. Where can he be?

Mason went to Grandma's big chair. A blanket was on the chair. The blanket made a lump. Was the lump the monkey? Mason pulled the blanket. The lump was only a pillow. But the pillow was on top of something. The blanket had been hiding it! There sat the monkey. "You were under the pillow!" said Mason. He gave the monkey a big hug.

Grandma laughed. "Shall we build a tower now?" she asked. Mason sat on the rug. He stacked one block, two blocks, three blocks. The monkey watched from his lap.

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Brooklyn went to the library with her mom. She wanted to find a book about ducks. On the shelf was a big rug with letters. Brooklyn sat down on the rug.

She put her hand on a letter. "B," her mom read. "B says buh." Brooklyn made the sound too. "Buh, buh, buh." Then she saw something. Her own name started with B. "B is for Brooklyn!" she said.

She looked for more B words around her. She saw a book. "Buh, book!" she said. She pointed at the rug. "Buh, bath rug! Ducks take baths." Her mom laughed a soft laugh. "Yes, they do," she said.

Brooklyn found the letter D next. "D," said Mom. "D says duh." Brooklyn looked around. "Duh, duck!" she said. There was a picture of a duck on the wall. The sun came in the window. It made the shiny duck picture shine.

Brooklyn picked out a duck book. At the desk, the librarian stamped it. "Bad weather is coming," the librarian said, looking at the gray sky. "Read fast." Brooklyn hugged her book. "Buh, book," she whispered. "Duh, duck." She held her mom's hand and they walked out the door together.

story:
Emile loved the truck book. It had a thick red cover and a flag on the first page. Miss Ada put the book in his hands. "You can take it home," she said. "Bring it back on Friday."

Emile looked at the pages. The letters sat under the pictures. Daddy ran his finger along them. "Truck," Daddy read. The word meant truck. Emile turned one page, then the next. The book went front to back, like a little road.

At school, Emile held the book tight. "Can I keep it forever?" he asked. Miss Ada shook her head. "Someone else wants a turn." Emile gave her the book. Ben smiled and took it. Emile found the shelf where the truck book lived. He put a small paper flag there. "That means my book," he said. Ben waved from the reading corner. "I will bring it back on Friday too."

story:
Ava sat at the dinner table. Her tummy made a little rumble. "I want my milk," she said. Mama poured the white milk into her cup. Ava drank it all up. "Look, my cup is empty now," she said.

After dinner, Mama ran the bath. Ava heard the water splash. She touched the bubbles with her toe. "So soft!" she said. The water washed the peas and the milk away. Now she was clean.

Mama put on her soft pajamas with cows on them. "The cow says moo," said Ava. Outside, the sky was dark and stormy. Rain tapped on the window. Ava yawned a big yawn. "Is it time for bed?" she asked. Mama kissed her head. "Yes, little one. Sleep now." Ava closed her eyes.

story:
Blake went to Mia's house. Mia had a music box. It played a song. "Let's clap!" said Mia.

Blake tried to clap. Her claps were too fast. Then her claps were too slow. She could not find the clapping. "I lose the song," said Blake.

Mia's mom put soap on her hands. She clapped the soap bubbles away. "Look," said Mia. Her claps went clap, clap, clap. They were steady, like walking feet.

Blake watched Mia's hands. She clapped when Mia clapped. Clap, clap, clap. Now her claps fit the song! "I did it!" said Blake. "It is easy now!"

Then they sang too. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Blake knew all the words. She sang the whole song all by herself.

The music box stopped. But Blake kept clapping and singing. "Again! Again!" she said.

Mia's mom wound the little key. The song began once more. "Our song!" said Blake.

knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Florence went to the library with her dad. She found a book about a little mouse. The cover had words on it. "Those words say The Tiny Mouse," said Dad. Florence opened the book. She turned the pages one by one. The story came in order, from the front to the back. At the end, the mouse found her home.

"I want to keep this book forever," said Florence.

"You can take it home," said Dad. "But we must bring it back. Other kids want to read it too."

Florence hugged the book. At home, she read it three times. The words stayed the same each time. On the last page, the mouse waved.

Then Florence put the book in her bag. "Time to go back," she said. She held Dad's hand all the way to the library, and set the book on the desk, ready for the next reader.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
story:
Hudson sat at the kitchen table. He wanted to paint a big brown bear. But there was no brown paint. He looked and looked. He only had red paint and yellow paint.

Hudson dipped his brush in the red. He made a spot on his paper. Then he dipped his brush in the yellow. He painted right on top of the red spot. The spot turned orange! Hudson's eyes got wide. He stirred the spot some more. It looked warm and brownish, just right for a sleepy bear.

He painted a big bear body. He painted soft round ears. Then Mom sprinkled salty salt over the wet paint. The salt made tiny sparkles, like stars on the bear. Hudson held his painting up to the light. "My bear can sleep under sparkly stars now," he said, and he laid the painting flat on the table to dry.
